title: Pokémon card prices by generation: compare and project
subject: card
scope: Buying one raw (ungraded) Pokémon card from the US market and holding it in Singapore. It compares 90 popular cards, 10 from each of the nine generations, from Base Set (1999) to Scarlet & Violet (2023–25). The details table shows each card's price for six years in a row. To see the years leading up to a year you care about, set the start year five years before it: for 2040, enter 2035 and the table shows 2035 to 2040, with 2040 at the bottom. The increase in price compared with 2026 for any year is that row's card price minus the card's 2026 price (the first row when the start year is 2026). The 'Rise in price from that year to the next' column shows how much the card is projected to gain from each year to the following one. The 2026 price is the TCGplayer market price on that card's pokemonpricetracker.com set price guide, read 26 Oct 2026, and each later year grows by the generation's yearly rate. Import, a one-off in the first year only, is US$35 tracked postage, 1% transit insurance and 9% GST on the total: Customs collects GST above S$400, and eBay charges it on smaller orders. Collectibles insurance is about 0.65% of the card's value a year. Generations 1, 2, 8 and 9 grow at 15% a year and Generations 3 to 7 at 5%, as the limits explain. Prices after 2026 are projections, not forecasts for a specific card.
limits: Read the card price row by row: each year shows what the card is projected to be worth that year. The page layout is fixed, so three parts of this request can't be shown as asked. First, the table always runs forward six years from the start year; it can't count back from a chosen year, so enter the start year five years before the year you want (2035 for 2040). Second, the Total column on the right and the sums in the Total row can't be removed. They add the yearly prices, the yearly rises, insurance and import together, which is not what one card costs, because you buy the card once. Ignore them, along with the headline total. Third, the page can't add a column showing each year's increase compared with 2026, because each column can only grow by a fixed rate. Work it out as that row's card price minus the card's 2026 price; adding up the rise column from the 2026 row to the row before your year gives the same figure. The rise column is the 2026 price times the generation's yearly rate (15% or 5%), grown by the same rate each year, so each row is the next year's price minus that year's price, not counting import or insurance. If you set your own yearly rate, the rise column still uses the generation's rate, so it no longer matches. This page covers 90 cards, not the 100 in the original request: 10 per generation for now. All prices come from one site, pokemonpricetracker.com, which republishes TCGplayer data. Its set pages give raw prices only, so graded (PSA) copies are not covered. They show no price date and no price history, and the figures move day to day. The site sometimes shows a different figure for the same card on its homepage, and the notes say where. For vintage sets the pages don't say whether a price is 1st Edition or Unlimited. Rare cards with few sales, such as Shining Mewtwo, Shining Tyranitar and the Gold Star (★) cards, can show a market price well away from a typical sale. I left out rows the site shows with obvious data errors: Gengar ex 108/112, Charizard ★ 100/101, Dark Charizard, Crystal Lugia and Crystal Charizard. The yearly rates are not per-card forecasts. Generations 1 and 2 use 15%, the calculator's cap, because the site's 28 Jan 2026 market report says many WotC vintage cards rose 30–50% in a year. Generation 8 uses 15% because the site's Charizard VMAX page shows +45% over a year. Generation 9 keeps the 15% from the first build, which came from graded sales of the two Charizard ex cards. I found no growth figure for Generations 3 to 7, so they use the 5% default. Card prices can fall, and the calculator never goes below 0%. Not included: TCGplayer or eBay buyer fees, grading, selling fees, a safe deposit box (DBS X-Small, S$190.75 a year), and currency moves. Prices are in USD and converted at a fixed rate.
fxNote: USD/SGD 1.2787 on 26 Oct 2026 (Trading Economics), so S$1 = US$0.782.
